# Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?

Miri Liu    Xiayu Zhao    Encheng Xie    ChengXiang Zhai
Affiliation: University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign
Affiliation: {miri3, xiayuz3, encheng2, czhai}@illinois.edu

###### Abstract

A major challenge facing AI scientific discovery pipelines is how to
determine when a generated idea is meaningfully novel. Ideally, novelty
checks in these pipelines must be able to reject non-novel ideas while
not rejecting too many novel ideas, and they should also be able to
distinguish which parts of a proposal are non-novel, as opposed to
opaquely discarding entire proposals. We design an analytical framework
for evaluation of novelty checks with temporal ground truth at both the
proposal- and claim-level, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals built
from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas matching
ones the field went on to publish. Auditing existing novelty checks with
this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on
non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are
later realized by human researchers, and observe that checks built to
evaluate proposals as a whole can point to claim-level prior art only by
rejecting the whole proposal. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a
fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module. ClaimNov catches
97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate, and its claim-level
novelty profile cuts the LLM judge’s false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%.
Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, ClaimNov also keeps
proposals that build on established contributions, rejecting only 3% of
ICLR-accepted proposals with a reviewer-disputed contribution and
keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced prior contribution,
against 76 for the strongest existing check. Code and data are available
at
[https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov](https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov).

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.36511v1/figs/teaser.jpg)

Figure 1: A useful novelty module must catch a non-novel copy while
keeping a novel idea. We reword $`n=95`$ published papers into 380
new-looking proposals (four disguises each) and plant the original
papers in the pool. Of these disguises
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Whole-Proposal Evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")),
ClaimNov correctly rejects 367 and names the source in 366, and it
rejects only 1.5% of the 400 later-realized ideas. We show ScholarEval
at its default rule (best threshold in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

The development of AI scientific discovery systems is an active,
fast-moving research field ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib27); [Yamada
et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Gottweis et al., 2026](#bib.bib15);
[Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)), and such systems have begun to
produce results that look like genuine, highly exciting discoveries
([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Sothanaphan, 2026](#bib.bib45); [Yoon
et al., 2026](#bib.bib60)). This is strong evidence that LLMs can be
creative, motivating their use in hypothesis generation ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib52); [Si et al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Liu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib24); [O’Neill et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)) and in
end-to-end discovery pipelines that generate, filter, and even execute
ideas autonomously or semi-autonomously ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib22);
[Baek et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Weng et al., 2025b](#bib.bib56);
[Ghareeb et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib48)).

One important facet of creativity, however, is novelty ([Ismayilzada
et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Lu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28)). Most AI
scientist pipelines employ some kind of novelty check (e.g., searching
against Semantic Scholar and using an LLM judge to determine if any
results are too close) which in turn decides which generated ideas will
go on to receive compute and human attention. Using a novelty check only
at the level of a whole proposal has three limitations. (1) Judging the
novelty of a whole proposal is challenging even for human experts; the
annotation itself is expensive and annotators often disagree about what
counts as novelty ([Si et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)). (2) Deployed checks
([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib27); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)) that
reject or pass a research proposal as a whole without considering its
parts subtly deviate from the tradition of human science, which is
incremental ([Uzzi et al., 2013](#bib.bib49)). (3) Whole-proposal checks
also make it harder, if not impossible, to understand whether they are
actually identifying the right prior work when they reject proposals. We
therefore argue that the right unit to consider is the claim, not the
proposal, since most papers, including ones that humans consider highly
novel, are not novel in literally every contribution they make ([Wang
et al., 2017](#bib.bib51)). With this motivation, we address the
limitations of previous work and make the following contributions to the
understanding and improvement of novelty checks in AI scientist
pipelines:

- •
  We introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable novelty module
  that treats claims as the basic unit of novelty.
- •
  We propose an evaluation framework for novelty checks in end-to-end AI
  scientist pipelines which draws upon temporal ground truth from the
  published record and from reviewer comments at a whole-proposal and
  claim-level, with four datasets totaling 1,060 proposals
  (§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Data Collection ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
- •
  We audit seven existing novelty checks alongside ClaimNov. The checks
  that reject the most non-novel work also reject the most work later
  realized by human researchers, and checks that judge proposals as a
  whole can only identify claim-level established work by rejecting an
  entire proposal.
- •
  ClaimNov catches 97% of disguised papers while rejecting only 1.5% of
  later realized ideas. It correctly preserves partially novel work,
  keeping 91 of 100 proposals with a spliced prior contribution against
  76 for the strongest existing check, and given the same attribution
  ranking, it keeps more correctly attributed proposals.

## 2 Related Work

Traditional measures of scientific novelty. [Zhao and Zhang
(2025)](#bib.bib62) categorize scientific novelty metrics by whether
they draw on citation data, textual data, or both. Bibliometric measures
use unusual or first-time combinations of cited work ([Uzzi et al.,
2013](#bib.bib49); [Wang et al., 2017](#bib.bib51); [Foster et al.,
2013](#bib.bib11)) or related ideas such as disruptiveness ([Wu et al.,
2019](#bib.bib57)); text-based measures consider semantic distance
([Shibayama et al., 2021](#bib.bib41); [Jeon et al., 2023](#bib.bib17))
or new concepts and new question–method combinations ([Mishra and
Torvik, 2016](#bib.bib31); [Luo et al., 2022](#bib.bib30)); some
measures also combine the two ([Amplayo et al., 2018](#bib.bib3)).
Traditional measures are often validated against external signals such
as expert judgments and later impact ([Bornmann et al.,
2019](#bib.bib7); [Fontana et al., 2020](#bib.bib10); [Arts et al.,
2021](#bib.bib5)). Our evaluation focuses on text-based measures, as
does our introduced module ClaimNov, which does not consider
bibliometric data.

Literature-grounded novelty assessment. Early on, IR and NLP researchers
studied novelty detection at the sentence and document level, as
information not covered by previously seen documents ([Soboroff and
Harman, 2005](#bib.bib44); [Ghosal et al., 2018](#bib.bib13); [Ghosal
et al., 2022](#bib.bib14)), and patent prior-art searches focused on
naming anticipating documents ([Piroi et al., 2011](#bib.bib35)). LLMs
have since enabled approaches that reason about the claims of existing
work: retrieving prior work to revise an idea ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib52)), judging a paper against retrieved neighbors ([Lin
et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)), reranking retrieved papers by idea-specific
facets ([Shahid et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)), scoring ideas against a
literature set ([Moussa et al., 2026](#bib.bib32); [Qiao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36)), and comparing atomic content units or contribution
claims against full-text evidence ([Ai et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib61); [Afzal et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). The typed
contribution claims used in ClaimNov draw on scientific information
extraction ([Luan et al., 2018](#bib.bib29); [D’Souza et al.,
2021](#bib.bib9)), facet-level views of ideas ([Radensky et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)) and claim verification ([Wadden et al.,
2020](#bib.bib50)). Benchmarks for these LLM-based systems score them
against expert annotations or review text ([Schopf and Färber,
2026](#bib.bib39); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib58)), against future papers
([Amplayo et al., 2019](#bib.bib4)), or under controlled, counterfactual
changes ([Liu and Zhai, 2026](#bib.bib26)). Critiques of LLM novelty
judges find that they prefer generated research questions that experts
rate lower ([Sinhahajari et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)) and that their
ratings disagree with hindsight against later papers ([Jiang,
2026](#bib.bib18)). We specifically evaluate novelty checks as deployed
inside AI-scientist pipelines, and also focus on counterfactual changes
rather than alignment with explicit human novelty labels, akin to how
paraphrase attacks test text detectors ([Krishna et al.,
2023](#bib.bib21)).

AI-scientist systems. Pipelines with a research-ideation stage almost
always include a novelty check for generated ideas, although these
checks can vary widely in mechanism
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
Some are hard filters grounded in retrieval, including AI Scientist’s
agentic search loop ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib27)), CoI-Agent’s
reject-and-regenerate loop ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)), the
retrieval filter of [Si et al. (2025)](#bib.bib42), and
AutoResearchClaw’s lexical check ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib25)).
Others are advisory or score-based, with or without explicit retrieval
([Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib59); [Baek et al., 2025](#bib.bib6);
[Gottweis et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Schmidgall et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Weng et al., 2025b](#bib.bib56); [Weng et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib55)); still others directly rank generated ideas against
one another ([Ghareeb et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Su et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46); [Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib48); [Keya et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20)). Work on automatic peer review usually judges full
papers, most recently with LLM judges ([Kang et al., 2018](#bib.bib19);
[Wang et al., 2020](#bib.bib53); [Taechoyotin and Acuna,
2025](#bib.bib47); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)); we instead focus
specifically on novelty.

## 3 Novelty Module

We introduce ClaimNov, an interpretable, claim-level novelty module for
research proposals that can be dropped directly into any AI for
scientific discovery pipeline with a novelty check. As shown in Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Evaluation Contract ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
ClaimNov extracts typed claims from research proposals, retrieves
relevant same-dimension claims from a pool of claims extracted from
prior art, scores the entailment per extracted claim, aggregates into a
novelty score, and passes the full claim profile to a verdict judge for
a binary novel or non-novel decision. For validation experiments, see
Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
and for exact prompts, see
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C ClaimNov Prompts ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").

### 3.1 Claim Extraction

During the claim extraction stage, ClaimNov takes the title and
description from the research proposal $`P`$ and produces, with an LLM
(gpt-4o-mini set to temperature 0), a list of contribution claims
$`C_{P}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{m}\}`$.

Each claim $`c_{i}`$ is typed with a dimension $`d_{c}`$ and an
attribute-value pair $`(c_{a},c_{v})`$. Dimensions are drawn from
$`\{`$Problem, Methodology, Resource, Result$`\}`$, while an attribute
represents the axis along which two works can be compared. For instance,
for a Result claim, the attribute may be classification accuracy on
CIFAR-10, and the value may be an improvement from 30.1% to 76.9%. We
aim to extract a small number of claims per proposal (2.4–2.7 on
average, the prompt allowing 1–4), based on conventions in AI research.
We process each paper in the reference pool $`\Pi`$ through this stage
once, using its abstract as the description text, to produce pool claims
$`C_{\Pi}`$.

### 3.2 Claim Retrieval

During the claim retrieval stage, ClaimNov takes a claim $`c`$ from the
previous stage’s list of claims, embeds its text together with its
paper’s title with text-embedding-3-large, and produces a set of
relevant pool claims $`R(c)`$ for comparison to that claim.

To obtain such a set, we retrieve the $`k`$-nearest (by cosine
similarity) pool claims of the same dimension, keeping at most one claim
per pool paper. We determine $`k`$ by pool size, taking $`k{=}10`$ as
the minimum based on an independent retrieval validation (see
Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")),
and for larger pools we use the heuristic $`k=0.2\,n_{d}`$, where
$`n_{d}`$ is the number of pool papers with a claim in that dimension,
capped at 40. This gives $`k{=}10`$ for the disguise pools and
$`k\approx 35`$ for the anchor pools
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Data Collection ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

### 3.3 Claim Entailment

During the claim entailment stage, ClaimNov judges the entailment of
every pair $`(c,c^{\prime})`$ for $`c^{\prime}\in R(c)`$ with an LLM
(gpt-4o-mini at temperature 0), giving titles and abstracts of pool
papers as context.

The judge rates the extent to which the pool claim entails or covers the
proposal claim on an ordinal scale
$`\ell(c,c^{\prime})\in\{1,\dots,5\}`$: 1 unrelated, 2 shared topic
only, 3 partial coverage with important details differing, 4 strong
coverage with minor details missing, and 5 full coverage of the claim’s
substantive content. We map these levels onto the unit interval by
taking $`e(c,c^{\prime})=(\ell(c,c^{\prime})-1)/4\in[0,1]`$.

### 3.4 Novelty Aggregation

During the novelty aggregation stage, we first take the sorted
$`e_{i}`$s from the previous stage and combine them into one coverage
score $`a(c)\in[0,1]`$ for each claim as a rank-discounted mean:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
a(c)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k_{c}}\alpha^{i-1}e_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{k_{c}}\alpha^{i-1}},\qquad\nu(c)\;=\;1-a(c),
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`\alpha{=}0.5`$, which balances the importance of the strongest
match against the weaker ones, and $`k_{c}=\min(k,|R(c)|)`$, which
prevents a claim with very few relevant pool claims from having an
inflated score.

We then combine claim scores into a proposal-level score using dimension
weights $`w_{d}`$ (Problem 0.4, Result 0.3, Methodology 0.2, Resource
0.1) and per-claim importance weights $`\mathrm{imp}(c)`$, which are
uniform for proposals and set to each claim’s share of support passages
when scoring a full paper. The dimension weights encode a prior about
contribution types in AI research; they can be tuned to adapt ClaimNov
to other fields.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A(P)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{c\in C_{P}}w_{d_{c}}\,\mathrm{imp}(c)\,a(c),`$ |  | (2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle A_{\max}(P)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{c\in C_{P}}w_{d_{c}}\,\mathrm{imp}(c),`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle N(P)`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-A(P)/A_{\max}(P).`$ |  |  |

$`A_{\max}(P)`$ is the coverage if every claim were fully covered.
$`N(P)`$ summarizes the novelty profile in one number; the full profile
is provided as context to the novelty verdict stage below.

### 3.5 Novelty Verdict

Finally, the novelty verdict stage of ClaimNov assembles previous
evidence produced by the module into a profile $`\Phi(P)`$ which is
evaluated by a stronger judge (claude-sonnet-4-6). $`\Phi(P)`$ lists the
proposal’s extracted claims with matched prior claims, their sources
(and their abstracts), and the entailment levels.

From the judge, we receive a verdict of pass or fail. If the proposal
fails, ClaimNov also outputs the prior art paper $`p^{\ast}\in\Pi`$, its
subset of claims $`S\subseteq C_{P}`$, and a one- or two-sentence
reason. For the exact prompt, please see
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C ClaimNov Prompts ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").

## 4 Experimental Setup

We explain the shared inputs and outputs for each check, which existing
checks we evaluate, the judge models and their temporal cutoffs, the
test data we collect, and the metrics we define.

### 4.1 Evaluation Contract

Because each of the AI scientist pipelines and standalone scientific
novelty evaluations we survey
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"))
uses slightly different schema, literature search, and verdict formats,
we standardize the evaluation contract to allow for better comparison.

We pass as input to each check a research proposal consisting of a title
plus a 150–400 word description as well as a reference pool, which is a
list of prior art papers given as
$`\{\text{id},\text{title},\text{abstract}\}`$. Checks using search are
sandboxed. For more details on how we adapt proposals to native input
formats, see
Table [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
For output, we consider three layers: L1, the verdict
$`\textit{verdict}\in\{\textit{pass},\textit{fail}\}`$ with reasons; L2,
a novelty score $`N(P)\in[0,1]`$; and L3, a novelty profile, every claim
with its matched prior claims, their entailment levels, and the papers
they come from. For ClaimNov, L3 determines both L2 and L1
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Novelty Aggregation ‣ 3 Novelty Module ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Novelty Verdict ‣ 3 Novelty Module ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
The existing checks we evaluate only emit L1.

![Refer to caption](2610.36511v1/figs/pipeline.png)

Figure 2: ClaimNov extracts typed contribution claims from a proposal
$`P`$, retrieves same-dimension claims from the pool, rates the extent
to which each covers $`P`$’s claims, aggregates these into one novelty
score, and gives a full claim-level novelty profile to a verdict judge.

### 4.2 Evaluated Systems

We consider four kinds of novelty check. (1) Novelty checks that are a
clear-cut component in some end-to-end AI-scientist pipeline: AI
Scientist v1 (check_idea_novelty), CoI-Agent (check_novel), Si et al.
(retrieve_novelty_score), and ARC’s lexical filter. (2) Novelty checks
we have “extracted” from pipelines that make some kind of novelty
judgment but which are not clearly plug-and-play in the same way:
ResearchAgent’s Originality rating (a proposal passes at a rating of 4
or 5 out of 5), ScholarEval’s pairwise contribution scoring (a proposal
passes when its mean score against the top-8 pool papers is positive),
and AI-Scientist-v2’s ideation reflection. The v2 ideation reflection
has no final verdict, so we append a final verdict to the prompt. (3) A
claim-level reference baseline after the style of OpenNovelty ([Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib61)), which judges 1–3 extracted contributions
against their BM25 top-10 and rejects when every contribution is
refuted. (4) ClaimNov as described in
§[3](#S3 "3 Novelty Module ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?") and its
ablations.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
gives our selection criteria and the full survey of 17 pipelines.
Searches embedded in novelty checks are replaced by dense retrieval over
the pool; see
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Adapter Details ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
for details.

### 4.3 Judge Models and Temporal Validity

Because six of the seven novelty checks we evaluate use an LLM as a
judge at some point (and ClaimNov also does so), we fix a cutoff $`T=`$
March 2026 and exclusively evaluate models with earlier cutoffs. This
mitigates the risk of models recognizing post-$`T`$ papers from training
data. We run each check with Sonnet 4.6 (training cutoff January 2026),
which is the same model ClaimNov uses as the final verdict judge (for
earlier, lightweight stages, ClaimNov uses gpt-4o-mini). As we explain
in more detail in
§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Data Collection ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
we use Sonnet 4.6 to generate ideas, disguise existing papers, and
rewrite disputed papers as research proposals, and Opus 4.6 (training
cutoff August 2025) as the labeler.

### 4.4 Data Collection

We collect data and establish ground truth for two levels of
non-novelty. In both cases, we aim to collect data that falls after our
temporal cutoff of $`T=`$ March 2026, to avoid LLM judge awareness.

#### Already-done ideas ($`n{=}400`$, whole-proposal level).

For this data, novelty checks should correctly reject a disguised
proposal if the source paper is in the pool, but should not reject when
the source is removed (making the proposal novel relative to the pool).
We collect $`n=100`$ ICML 2026 spotlight papers, filtering for papers
where the v1 arXiv appeared after $`T`$, and disguise each paper as a
new research proposal at four increasingly challenging to spot levels of
disguise. Rung 1 swaps the voice, rung 2 paraphrases, rung 3 reframes
the paper with a different motivation, reordered contributions, and an
unnamed method, and rung 4 restructures it adversarially from a
different theoretical starting point with generalized numbers. Because
rungs 3 and 4 may depart significantly from the original paper, we
accept them only when a verifier (Sonnet 4.6) confirms that the core
contributions are the same. To ensure the disguise is challenging, we
require that at most 2% of the disguise’s 6-grams appear in the source,
regenerating up to three times; for more details and prompts, see
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Disguise Prompts ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
We then form a reference pool from the source plus up to 19 pre-$`T`$
papers closest to the proposal by embedding, which we take from the
source’s reference list and Semantic Scholar recommendations. We drop
five sources whose pools contain only the source, leaving 380 disguises
(all 400 in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

#### Claim-disputed ideas ($`n{=}160`$, claim level).

For this data, novelty checks should correctly find a prior work $`B`$
that establishes a specific claim. We use a regex prefilter and
gpt-5-nano classification to mine 8.3k ICLR 2022–23 reviews in which a
reviewer identified a paper $`A`$’s contribution as already established
by some prior paper $`B`$. We then rewrite each $`A`$ in proposal voice
with Sonnet 4.6 and the rung-1 prompt provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Disguise Prompts ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
and plant $`B`$ among 19 pre-$`T`$ papers to serve as distractors. We
also record the final ICLR decision (62 accepted, 96 rejected, 2
unknown) as an additional axis of analysis of novelty check performance.
Of $`n=200`$ pairs of papers $`(A,B)`$, we keep $`n=160`$ with usable
pools, and we annotate a sample for genuine disputes (see
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Label Validation ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
Unlike the other sets, these papers predate $`T`$ and may appear in a
judge’s training data. In this case the ground truth is reviewer
attribution (and not some post-$`T`$ event), so we consider this
acceptable.

#### Later-realized ideas ($`n{=}400`$, whole-proposal level).

For this data, novelty checks should correctly pass the proposal,
because the pool does not contain the idea and researchers went on to
realize some of its contributions. We collect $`n{=}30`$ anchor papers,
where each anchor paper was published in NeurIPS 2025 proceedings and
has at least 50 citing papers that fall after $`T`$. We exclude
benchmarks, datasets, and surveys (which may be cited primarily for
use), then generate new proposals based on the remaining anchor
abstracts. We construct a relevant works pool (median 174 papers, capped
at 400 papers) for each anchor from its reference list plus any citing
papers that come before $`T`$, as well as a follow-up pool $`F`$ of the
citing papers that come after $`T`$ (median 124 papers). We use each
anchor paper to generate $`n{=}100`$ ideas from Sonnet 4.6, producing
$`n{=}3000`$ proposals total. For each of these proposals, Opus 4.6
writes a contribution list, then labels each contribution as established
or not by the 8 papers in the pool nearest to the idea (by
text-embedding-3-small over title and abstract) and, separately, by the
8 nearest papers in $`F`$. We identify later-realized ideas as proposals
with at least one contribution established in $`F`$ and none established
in the pool. From the 407 proposals of this kind generated from 26 of
the 30 anchors, we draw 400 at random to constitute this dataset. We
provide labeling prompts in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Later-Realized Labeling Prompts ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").

#### Hybrid proposals ($`n{=}100`$, claim level).

For this data, novelty checks should correctly pass the proposal and
correctly name the paper whose contribution it contains. We take
$`n=100`$ later-realized (and thus assumed novel) ideas from the
previous dataset and, for each, a pool paper $`B`$ which was moderately
similar (ranked 5–15 by cosine similarity), then ask Sonnet 4.6 to
rewrite these ideas so that $`B`$’s core contribution is also included.
Sonnet 4.6 verifies that the splice preserved the original contributions
while adding the new one.

### 4.5 Metrics

We evaluate based on two levels of granularity – the whole-proposal
level and the claim level – motivated by the idea that we want to reject
proposals that are wholly non-novel, but not proposals that simply
contain some existing claims.

For the whole-proposal level, we evaluate checks’ ability to catch
non-novel ideas as well as their false alarm rate, how often they reject
ideas that are later realized and validated by the human researcher
community. We measure false alarms both on the later-realized ideas (FA)
and, as a second set of assumed novel ideas, on the disguises with their
source removed from the pool (Src. out). From these, we compute
informedness $`\textbf{J}=\text{catch}-\text{FA}`$ and the pool-flip
$`\bm{\Delta}=\text{catch}-\text{Src.\ out}`$, or the drop in rejection
rate when the disguised proposal’s source paper is removed from the
pool.

For both whole-proposal and claim level, we evaluate checks’ ability to
attribute claims to prior art. For whole-proposal, we observe whether
checks name the source paper for disguises, and for claim level, we
report the share of the $`n{=}160`$ claim-disputed proposals for which a
check’s top-ranked paper is the prior art $`B`$. We also report
rejection rates on this set by ICLR decision, with the motivation that
one disputed claim does not a non-novel proposal make.

## 5 Results

We find that ClaimNov is both sensitive and specific, catching disguised
copies of published work while keeping ideas that researchers went on to
publish
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Whole-Proposal Evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, we also find that
ClaimNov preserves proposals in which a single contribution is
established, so more correctly attributed proposals can reach the full
AI-scientist pipeline
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Claim-Level Prior Art ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Hybrid Proposals ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
We report full results in
Tables [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Whole-Proposal Evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")–[3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Hybrid Proposals ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
with 95% intervals and paired exact McNemar tests in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Intervals and Paired Tests ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").

On whole proposals
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Whole-Proposal Evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")),
all checks except ARC and ScholarEval catch at least 338 of 380
disguises, but most checks continue to reject after the source is
removed. For instance, Si et al. catches all 380 but also rejects 359
when the source is no longer present in the pool. All checks except
ClaimNov and CoI-Agent also reject a large share of ideas the field went
on to publish. Si et al. rejects 96%, ResearchAgent 98.5%, AI
Scientist v1 52%, and AI-Scientist-v2 39%. ARC and ScholarEval reject
0.0%, but do so by rejecting almost nothing.

ClaimNov and CoI-Agent are clear outliers in their ability to balance
the two. Both catch almost every disguise (367 and 368 of 380,
respectively) while rejecting few later-realized ideas (1.5% and 3.8%).
ClaimNov has the highest $`J`$ ($`+0.95`$) and $`\Delta`$ ($`+0.92`$),
whereas the next best pipeline checks after CoI-Agent are at $`+0.56`$
and $`+0.76`$. The per-contribution OpenNovelty-style baseline does
catch more disguises (379, $`p{<}.001`$) but false-alarms on 11.5% of
later-realized ideas and rejects 38 disguises with the source removed
($`p{=}.001`$ against ClaimNov). While clustering tests by source and
anchor shows ClaimNov and CoI-Agent are statistically level, ClaimNov’s
verdict call costs a quarter of CoI-Agent’s check call with the same
judge (\$0.010 against \$0.039), with entailment cost growing with pool
size
(Table [9](#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M In-the-Loop Pilot ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

The ClaimNov ablations
(Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H ClaimNov Ablations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"))
show the value of each stage of the module. Without the claim-level
novelty profile, the verdict judge reads the nearest abstracts instead,
and its false-alarm rate rises from 1.5% to 11.8% as a result. When we
instead use a per-claim verdict rule, which fails a proposal if any
central claim appears entailed, we catch all 380 disguised proposals,
but the false-alarm rate rises to 56.8% and we wrongly reject 197 of the
380 proposals whose source has been removed. This reinforces the idea
that (1) claims are the appropriate unit for understanding a research
proposal and (2) a research proposal is not one large claim; its claims
should be considered separately. On generated ideas that a whole-idea
labeler matched to one pool paper, ClaimNov rejects 18%, against 55% for
the judge without the claim-level novelty profile
(Appendix [L](#A12 "Appendix L Natural Already-Done Ideas ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
These ideas are noisier than disguises, and we audit a sample of them by
hand, together with later-realized ideas, in
Appendix [F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Audit of generated ideas ‣ Appendix F Label Validation ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
Results with other verdict judges are given in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").

acc./Rej. rej.: rejection rate on the 62 ICLR-accepted and 96

Names $`B`$: share whose top-ranked paper is the reviewer’s $`B`$. On

We evaluate ClaimNov and the seven existing checks on claim-level data
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Claim-Level Prior Art ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"))
and find that ClaimNov correctly treats a disputed claim as a
claim-level finding, and not a reason to reject an entire research
proposal. It rejects only 3% of accepted ICLR proposals, the lowest rate
of any check that catches disguises (10% for CoI-Agent and 47–81% for Si
et al., AI Scientist v1, and ResearchAgent). All of the whole-proposal
checks we evaluate name prior art only alongside a rejection, so Si et
al. names $`B`$ for 47% by rejecting about 80% of proposals, and
CoI-Agent passes 89%, meaning it can name $`B`$ for only the remaining
11%.

Considering this design choice in existing checks, we separate
attribution from the verdict by pairing each verdict with the same
attribution ranking. ClaimNov’s top-rated profile paper is $`B`$ for 21%
of proposals, while the pool paper nearest to the whole proposal by
dense embedding is $`B`$ for 37%. Intuitively, this is because the $`B`$
named by a reviewer is often closest to the proposal as a whole, which
embedding similarity captures well, whereas ClaimNov ranks papers by how
fully they cover a single extracted claim. Extraction failures further
exacerbate this issue
(Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Attribution by Dimension and Relation Type ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
We therefore pass the dense ranking to every verdict, and ClaimNov then
passes the proposal and names $`B`$ for 36% of proposals, against 31%
for CoI-Agent ($`p{=}.016`$). Given the same attribution, ClaimNov’s
verdict keeps more proposals building on established work.

Evaluating ClaimNov alongside the existing checks on the hybrid
proposals
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Hybrid Proposals ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"))
allows us to more clearly distinguish ClaimNov’s advantages. We fix the
correct behavior by construction, as each proposal is a later-realized
novel idea which should not be rejected, and we control proper
attribution by splicing in a contribution from a known paper $`B`$. The
other checks continue to behave roughly according to established traits.
ARC and ScholarEval pass all 100 and name nothing, Si et al. names $`B`$
for 63 but rejects all 100, and ResearchAgent rejects 98. CoI-Agent, the
closest check on whole proposals, passes 76 and names $`B`$ for only 11
of the 100, all among the 24 it rejects.

ClaimNov, on the other hand, passes 91 of 100 ($`p{=}.004`$ against
CoI-Agent). Because a hybrid states $`B`$’s contribution explicitly,
BM25 over the whole proposal ranks $`B`$ first for 74. Given this shared
ranking (similarly to the isolation we perform in
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Claim-Level Prior Art ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")),
ClaimNov keeps 67 hybrids with $`B`$ named, against 53 for CoI-Agent
($`p{=}.004`$). The OpenNovelty-style baseline keeps 64, but this is at
the cost of 11.5% false alarms on later-realized ideas
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Whole-Proposal Evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
When ClaimNov successfully extracts the spliced claim as its own claim
(as opposed to missing it or absorbing it into a different claim), the
entailment judge rates $`B`$ at level 4 or 5, and the verdict stage
properly reads one established claim among several novel ones as a
proposal that builds on prior work. We consider these ratings reliable,
as 13 of the 15 papers rated at level 4 or above are $`B`$, and this
entailment level is reached by only 9 of 400 later-realized ideas
(Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Intervals and Paired Tests ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

## 6 Conclusion

We establish an evaluation framework with temporal ground truth at both
the proposal and the claim level, and use it to audit seven existing
novelty checks. We find that the checks which reject the most non-novel
work also tend to reject the most work the field went on to publish, and
observe that checks built to judge proposals as a whole name claim-level
prior art only when they reject. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a
drop-in claim-level novelty module, and show it rejects non-novel ideas,
keeps novel and partially novel ones, and, given the same attribution
ranking, keeps more correctly attributed proposals. Beyond filtering, a
specific claim-level check like ClaimNov could serve as a reward when
training AI-scientist agents, since it does not penalize the incremental
follow-ups most science consists of, and its profile tells the agent
which of its contributions are new. Do AI scientists know what’s new?
Based on current novelty checks, they largely do not, rejecting much of
what the field goes on to publish or practically nothing at all.
However, ClaimNov enables scientific novelty to be judged claim by claim
against specific prior papers, thus potentially making AI scientists
much better judges of novelty.

## Limitations

Our work employs several heuristics in how we consider sets of proposals
or papers to be novel or non-novel, and this is not as clean as if we
had a “true” dataset. We also focus exclusively on AI research. In
practice, this is where most AI-scientist work also concentrates, so
this aligns well, but if we want AI-scientist pipelines to be more
widely applicable, then assumptions like the ones we make about
dimension weights (problem contributions being more valuable than other
contributions, for instance) might not generalize and would require
further tuning for different fields, thus impeding adoption. We also
consider only English-language research, which can further skew
generalization.

Because our pools are fixed lists of prior work rather than open search,
consisting of 20 papers for disguises and disputed pairs and up to 400
for generated ideas, we have limited ability to evaluate the retrieval
of novelty checks. Additionally, we identify later-realized ideas with
an LLM labeler, although we do cross-check this with a different model
family labeler and with a small-scale human audit in
Appendix [F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Audit of generated ideas ‣ Appendix F Label Validation ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
Our disguised proposals and generated ideas are generated by the same
model (Sonnet 4.6) that ultimately judges, which is a known source of
possible bias for LLMs-as-judges ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib63);
[Panickssery et al., 2024](#bib.bib34)).

The temporal construction of our datasets also decays, since running the
same analysis with more recent LLM judges (with training cutoffs
post-$`T`$) will require all materials to be rebuilt at a later $`T`$.
Although this is simple mechanically and our scripts support it, this
still takes time and money. Finally, one important aspect of novelty
modules in AI-scientist pipelines is how they affect in-the-loop
generation: when the module is actively rejecting and causing
regeneration of proposals, how does that affect the final committed set
of ideas, and what are the compute and token costs involved? We leave
this question to future work because (1) it is highly computationally
expensive compared to the static question we examine and (2)
establishing ground truth for ideas produced in response to a rejection
is harder still and may require extensive human annotation, for which we
have limited resources. We do run a small pilot
(Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M In-the-Loop Pilot ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"))
and report the rejection and cost dynamics of the loop.

## Ethical Considerations

Our aim with this work is to encourage the development of scientific
novelty modules in AI scientist pipelines which are better aligned with
human understandings of novelty, which we believe is important to the
science produced by these pipelines. We recognize that development of AI
for scientific discovery capabilities has several concerning
implications for current review processes and for the human experience
of science in general. ClaimNov, like any automated judge, should be
used carefully.

We do not release any intellectual property directly; we release no
direct paper text, only pointers and code for reproduction of our
results, and we do not release ICLR review text, but rather the code
that re-mines the claim disputes from OpenReview. We follow the terms of
use of both arXiv and OpenReview licenses. Additionally, while we use
human annotation to validate some LLM labels, the annotation consists
only of labels on published papers and generated ideas, and we collect
no survey responses or personal information. It is not human-subjects
research and falls outside IRB review.

## Appendix A Pipeline Survey

Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
surveys the novelty judgments embedded in AI-scientist pipelines, and
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
lists standalone novelty judges.
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
shows what each pipeline passes downstream after its check, which shapes
the evaluation contract
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Evaluation Contract ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
gives the systems we include and exclude. We include a system when (1)
its code is available, (2) it has a separable judgment call, (3) that
judgment takes a research proposal as input, (4) we can control the
reference pool or sandbox its retrieval, and (5) its judge can be
replaced with one whose training cutoff predates $`T`$.
Table [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
shows how the shared proposal is passed to each included check, and
Table [9](#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix A Pipeline Survey ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
gives the measured cost of the final judge calls.

|  System |  Where judgment sits |  Input artifact $`I`$ |  Pool at judgment time |  Output $`O`$ and enforcement |  Pool controllable? |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  AI Scientist v1 ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib27)) |  Hard post-ideation filter (check_idea_novelty) |  Idea dict: Name, Title, Experiment (2–4 sentences), 1–10 self-ratings; task description and template code |  Agentic loop, $`\leq`$10 rounds $`\times`$ 10 Semantic Scholar hits (title, abstract, venue, year, citations) |  novel: bool parsed from a literal “Decision made”; non-novel ideas discarded; no decision after 10 rounds $`\Rightarrow`$ not novel |  Yes: one search_for_papers(); replace check_idea_novelty wholesale |
|  AI Scientist v2 ([Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib59)) |  No separable check; advisory retrieval inside ideation reflections |  Search-query strings; idea JSON (Name, Title, Short Hypothesis, Related Work, Abstract $`\approx`$250w, Experiments) |  Same endpoint, top-10, citation-sorted |  Nothing machine-readable; lands as Related Work prose; a human picks the idea to run |  Yes: use_tool(query) is the single chokepoint |
|  CoI-Agent ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)) |  Hard filter plus uncapped regeneration loop |  One free-text blob (motivation, novelty, method merged; structure dissolved before the check) |  $`\leq`$3 LLM queries $`\times`$ 5 hits, title+abstract; date cutoff and ban list built in |  Binary \<similar\> plus offending paper and summary, fed back to regeneration; criterion near plagiarism-strength identity; empty retrieval $`\Rightarrow`$ novel |  Yes: check_novel has a clean signature |
|  Si et al. ([Si et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)) |  (a) intra-batch embedding dedup; (b) Swiss tournament, novelty excluded; (c) retrieval filter, the real check |  (a) title + 5 fields; (c) full proposal JSON (Problem, Existing Methods, Motivation, Proposed Method, Experiment Plan; 1–2 pages) |  (a) own ideas only, MiniLM cosine $`>0.8`$; (c) top-10 abstracts via LLM keyword queries |  (a) drop duplicates (4000 $`\to`$ $`\approx`$200); (c) per-paper binary “same problem and same approach?”; any yes rejects, evidence attached |  Yes: retrieve_novelty_score, or pre-populate the paper list |
|  ResearchAgent ([Baek et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) |  Soft critic in generate $`\to`$ validate $`\to`$ refine $`\times`$3, per artifact (problem, method, experiment) |  Artifact plus rationale; grounding context (core paper, references without abstracts, entity store) |  No retrieval at review time; frozen jsonl pool from generation |  Originality 1–5 Likert plus feedback; steers refinement and best-of-$`N`$; never rejects |  Yes (fully): static pool; swap the originality prompt |
|  Agent Laboratory ([Schmidgall et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)) |  No check; lit review judges relevance; post-hoc reviewer scores the finished paper |  Topic string (review); full LaTeX (reviewer) |  arXiv top-5 (review); parametric (reviewer) |  Originality 1–4 inside a NeurIPS-style review JSON; revision feedback and solver reward; never checks pre-experiment |  Yes: ArxivSearch swappable; insert a phase |
|  SCI-IDEA ([Keya et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)) |  Mid-pipeline “Aha” filter |  1–2 sentence idea, SciBERT-embedded |  None; novelty $`=1-\max`$ cosine to sibling candidates, surprise $`=-\log p`$ |  Continuous scores $`\to`$ binary flag; only flagged ideas refined |  No code released |
|  CycleResearcher ([Weng et al., 2025a](#bib.bib55)) |  Post-hoc whole-paper review; reward for RL loop |  Full paper ($`\approx`$14k tokens) |  Parametric (fine-tuned on ICLR reviews) |  Review dict (ratings, contribution, decision); no novelty field |  No: monolithic fine-tune; a module must sit upstream |
|  DeepScientist ([Weng et al., 2025b](#bib.bib56)) |  Valuation against own findings memory (paper); prompt-file check (repo) |  Hypothesis record; repo: draft template (claim, closest prior work, novelty type) |  Own findings archive; literature via mandated sweep ($`\geq`$5 closest papers) |  $`\langle`$utility, quality, exploration$`\rangle`$ 0–100 drives compute (paper); 0/1/2 novelty rubric, $`<7`$ blocks promotion (repo) |  Yes (repo): editable markdown check; paper’s scoring code not public |
|  Robin ([Ghareeb et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)) |  Novelty is one of five criteria in pairwise ranking, after per-candidate lit reports |  Hypothesis name plus 800–1500w literature report; judged in pairs |  Literature baked into the report upstream; parametric at judge time |  Pairwise winner $`\to`$ Bradley–Terry strength; nothing discarded; orders for human wet-lab pick |  Indirect: pool fixed before the judge; swap the pair comparison |
|  AI-Researcher ([Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib48)) |  “Pick the most novel of 5”; no similarity computed |  Five markdown ideas (1–3k words) in one prompt |  Seeded reference papers and repos on disk; search tools disabled |  Free text: one selected idea report; the other four silently dropped; no score persisted |  Yes: per-task reference list; replace the selection call |
|  ARC ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib25)) |  Stage-08 lexical check, explicitly non-blocking |  Topic plus hypotheses.md (H1–H4, 300–1200w) plus seen-paper rows |  Live search ($`\leq`$5 queries $`\times`$ 15; OpenAlex, S2, arXiv) $`\cup`$ Stage-04 candidates; titles+abstracts |  Keyword-Jaccard score 0–1, band, recommendation in {proceed, differentiate, abort}; advisory to a human |  Yes: pass papers_already_seen or shadow check_novelty() |
|  SciMON ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib52)) |  Retrieve $`\to`$ compare $`\to`$ rewrite loop after initial generation |  Idea plus background and problem context |  Top-20 idea sentences from the training set (SentenceBERT) |  LLM rewrites the idea until similarity falls below a threshold |  Yes: all modules explicit |
|  Idea Novelty Checker ([Shahid et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)) |  Generate $`\to`$ check $`\to`$ replace facet $`\to`$ regenerate |  Idea decomposed into domain, purpose, mechanism, evaluation facets |  Top-100 embedding-filtered papers (ideation, semantic search, related work), RankGPT top-10 |  Binary label plus explanation and alternative facet; human may override |  Yes: separate stages; new papers injectable before reranking |
|  VirSci ([Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)) |  Relative-novelty voting plus self-review of the finished abstract |  Idea description, experiment, self-rating |  Pre-cutoff papers (title, abstract, citations); per-idea retrieval |  Preferred candidate plus reasoning; plurality vote selects the one idea written up |  Yes: pool replaceable |
|  AI Co-Scientist ([Gottweis et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) |  Fast initial review, then literature-grounded full review |  Hypothesis or proposal plus parsed goal, constraints, and whether novelty is required |  Parametric (initial); web search or scientist-provided repository (full) |  Non-novel hypotheses discarded at initial review; full review summarizes known work as the comparison |  Partly: provided pool replaceable, web search is not fixed |

Table 4: Novelty judgments embedded in surveyed AI-scientist pipelines.
Pool controllable: where an external module can replace the native
judgment.

|  System |  Judges what |  Input $`I`$ |  Pool |  Output $`O`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  RAG-Novelty ([Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)) |  Published papers |  Title and abstract plus two retrieval scalars (mean neighbor date, mean cosine); neighbors never reach the prompt |  Own vector store ($`\approx`$12k per field), $`k{=}10`$, pre-date filter; fully swappable |  Integer 1–10 plus justification |
|  OpenNovelty ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib61)) |  Full papers |  PDF $`\to`$ core task and 1–3 contribution claims |  Proprietary search API; top-50 per task, top-10 per contribution; citation index is the injection point |  Per contribution: can refute / cannot refute / unclear, with evidence and summary; no numeric score |
|  NovaScore ([Ai et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) |  News documents |  Document $`\to`$ atomic content units |  Unit bank (SBERT, top-5, $`\geq`$0.6); experimenter-defined |  Per-unit binary novelty $`\times`$ salience $`\to`$ $`[0,1]`$ aggregate |
|  InnoEval ([Qiao et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)) |  Research ideas |  Six-tuple (TLDR, motivations, questions, methods, settings, results), auto-extracted |  Six-source search, top-10 per category; swappable searchers |  0–10 per dimension incl. novelty, five personas, mean plus accept-tier label |
|  ScholarEval ([Moussa et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)) |  Research ideas |  Research plan, with comparison dimensions extracted from it |  Retrieved literature; swappable |  Contribution arm: pairwise score against each retrieved paper per dimension, averaged to $`-10`$ to $`+10`$; no accept threshold |

|  System |  Committed idea artifact (post-check, pre-execution) |  Where captured |  What runs on it |
|----|----|----|----|
|  AI Scientist v1 |  Idea dict (Name, Title, Experiment), novelty-filtered |  ideas.json per template |  experiments $`\to`$ full paper |
|  AI Scientist v2 |  Idea JSON incl. Short Hypothesis, Related Work, Abstract, Experiments |  ideas JSON; human picks an index |  tree-search experiments $`\to`$ paper |
|  CoI-Agent |  final_idea free-text blob |  return value of the regeneration loop |  experiment design |
|  Si et al. |  Full proposal JSON (7 fields incl. test cases, fallback plan) |  top_ideas.json, rank-ordered and filter-passed |  human study / execution study |
|  ResearchAgent |  Problem, method, experiment design, each with rationale; best-of-$`N`$ |  pipeline history, max-score pick |  (idea is the end product) |
|  Agent Laboratory |  Research plan from plan formulation |  agent state |  experiments $`\to`$ paper |
|  SCI-IDEA |  Refined “Aha” idea text |  module-2 output |  (idea is the end product) |
|  CycleResearcher |  None exposed; output is a full paper |  LaTeX |  review $`\to`$ RL reward |
|  DeepScientist |  Promoted hypothesis record (claim plus valuation vector) |  findings memory |  expensive validation runs |

## Appendix B Adapter Details

We pass the same (proposal, pool) pair to each check. For all checks
that do some kind of search, we sandbox the search, ranking the pool by
cosine similarity (text-embedding-3-large) to the query (checks can
still use their native query style and specified depth $`k`$). In all
cases, we set the final judge to Sonnet 4.6 at temperature 0
(Table [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix B Adapter Details ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
In the OpenNovelty-style baseline, we reimplement the per-contribution
design of [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib61) with BM25 retrieval to avoid
sharing a retriever with ClaimNov. BM25 throughout is rank_bm25’s
BM25Okapi with default parameters ($`k_{1}{=}1.5`$, $`b{=}0.75`$) over
lowercased alphanumeric tokens with stopwords removed, and the
scientific embeddings are SciNCL (malteos/scincl) and SPECTER2
(allenai/specter2_base with the proximity adapter).

|  Check |  Search into pool |  Decision rule |
|----|----|----|
|  AI Sci. v1 |  up to 10 rounds, each one LLM query $`\to`$ top-10 |  “Decision made: not novel” rejects; no decision after 10 rounds rejects (shipped default) |
|  CoI-Agent |  up to 3 LLM queries $`\to`$ top-5 each, deduplicated |  \<similar\>1 rejects and names a paper; empty retrieval passes (shipped) |
|  Si et al. |  1–3 keyword queries plus the title $`\to`$ top-10 each |  papers scored 1–10, the top 5 checked one by one, any “same problem and approach” rejects |
|  ARC |  whole pool, no LLM |  keyword Jaccard and title similarity $`\geq 0.25`$ for some paper rejects |
|  ResearchAgent |  proposal $`\to`$ top-10 titles |  Originality rating $`\leq 3`$ of 5 rejects (no native threshold; shipped temperature 1.25 not kept) |
|  ScholarEval |  proposal $`\to`$ top-8 |  mean pairwise score over the 8 papers $`\leq 0`$ rejects (no native threshold) |
|  AI-Sci.-v2 |  proposal $`\to`$ top-10 |  reflection prompt plus an appended NOVELTY: pass/fail slot |
|  OpenNov.-style |  1–3 extracted contributions $`\to`$ BM25 top-10 each |  one judge call over all contributions; rejects when every contribution is can_refute (rejecting on any raises false alarms to 55.8%) |

Table 10: Sandboxed search and decision rule of each adapter.

## Appendix F Label Validation

For $`n{=}100`$ pairs of papers $`A`$ and $`B`$ where an LLM identified
a prior-art dispute, two annotators independently mark (i) whether the
dispute is genuine, (ii) whether the extracted $`B`$ is the correct
prior art, and (iii) the dispute type. They achieve (i) 81/100 raw
agreement with Cohen’s $`\kappa=0.62`$, (ii) 73/100 and
$`\kappa{=}0.47`$, and (iii) 52/100 and $`\kappa{=}0.40`$, and we drop
the dispute-type labels due to the low kappa value. A third annotator
then marked the 63 rows with any disagreements, blinded to the labels of
the first two annotators. By 2-of-3 majority we find that we have 59/100
genuine disputes with 67/100 having correctly-identified $`B`$. We use
the 40 pairs that have a genuine dispute and correct $`B`$ as the
label-clean subset, 36 of which have usable pools
(Table [12](#A6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix F Label Validation ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
All three annotators have graduate-level education in English in the
relevant research field.

| Question                       | Agreement | $`\bm{\kappa}`$ |
|--------------------------------|-----------|-----------------|
| Dispute is genuine             | 81/100    | .62             |
| $`B`$ is the correct prior art | 73/100    | .47             |
| Dispute type (dropped)         | 52/100    | .40             |

Table 11: Raw agreement and Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ between the first two
annotators.

| Check           | Rej. acc. | Rej. rej. | Names $`B`$    |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| AI Scientist v1 | 7/16      | 7/19      | —              |
| CoI-Agent       | 2/16      | 3/19      | —              |
| Si et al.       | 14/16     | 14/19     | 19, rejecting  |
| OpenNov.-style  | 2/16      | 3/19      | —              |
| ClaimNov        | 1/16      | 1/19      | 15, 14 passing |

### F.1 Audit of generated ideas

We audit 60 generated ideas by hand with the second set of instructions
above, one annotator per item. These are 45 later-realized ideas (25 at
random, 10 that the whole-idea Opus pass called already done, and 10
that a low-false-alarm check rejected) and 15 sorter-matched ideas. This
labeling is extremely strenuous, since each item requires reading an
idea against 20 abstracts and deciding whether any one paper does
substantially the same thing, a judgment on which experts often disagree
([Si et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)). Annotators confirm 28 of the 45
later-realized ideas as novel relative to the pool (a stratum-weighted
60% of all 400) and judge 9 of the 15 sorter-matched ideas already done.
Table [13](#A6.T13 "Table 13 ‣ F.1 Audit of generated ideas ‣ Appendix F Label Validation ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
gives each check’s rejections on both groups of later-realized ideas. On
the 9 sorter-matched ideas judged already done, ClaimNov with fixed
retrieval depth rejects 1 and the w/o-profile judge 7, which also
rejects 3 of the 6 judged novel.

## Appendix H ClaimNov Ablations

We explain the ablations we evaluate for ClaimNov. Each aims to ablate
one stage, leaving the rest unchanged
(Table [15](#A8.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix H ClaimNov Ablations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

|  Ablation |  Change from full ClaimNov |
|----|----|
|  W/o claim profile |  the verdict stage (same model, prompt) reads eight pool abstracts nearest to the proposal by embedding instead of the novelty profile |
|  W/o verdict judge (graded check) |  fail when aggregate score $`N(P)<0.5`$ or any claim is covered at level 4 or higher by one prior claim |
|  Per-claim verdict rule |  one judge call per candidate paper on whether it establishes the central claim; any yes fails |
|  Fixed depth ($`k{=}10`$) |  the 10 nearest same-dimension prior claims for every claim, disregarding pool size |

Table 15: ClaimNov ablations.

## Appendix K Robustness

In this section, we test some assumptions to better understand if our
main results depend on our specific labels, judge model, pool sizes, or
the particular data we collected.

Because our later-realized labels come from one Opus labeler, we
recompute false alarms under three alternative labelers in
Table [23](#A11.T23 "Table 23 ‣ Reproducibility. ‣ Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
specifically (1) a labeler from a different model family (gpt-5), (2)
the ideas both Opus and gpt-5 agree on, and (3) the full set without the
$`n=101`$ ideas a whole-idea Opus labeling pass considered previously
done. For all of these labeling paradigms, ClaimNov’s false-alarm rate
stays between 1.3% and 1.5%.

We check whether the claim-level novelty profile we provide for our
final verdict is only helpful to our particular judge (Sonnet 4.6) by
rerunning this stage with two non-Anthropic judges, specifically
gpt-oss-120b (117B parameters) and Llama 4 Maverick (17B active, 400B
total) in
Table [24](#A11.T24 "Table 24 ‣ Reproducibility. ‣ Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
These are weaker models, so catch does drop, but we still observe as
with Sonnet that providing the profile cuts false alarms and source-out
rejections relative to the base judge reading nearest abstracts.

We check in
Table [25](#A11.T25 "Table 25 ‣ Reproducibility. ‣ Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
whether baselines can match the judged checks. These are thresholds on
lexical or embedding similarity, a judge that sees only the single
nearest paper, and the extracted score-based checks at their best
threshold. The baselines are not competitive with ClaimNov’s $`J`$.

Because our disguise pools hold only 20 papers, in
Table [26](#A11.T26 "Table 26 ‣ Reproducibility. ‣ Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
we artificially increase the pool size to $`\approx 200`$ to investigate
if our catch can survive more realistic pool sizes. While catch does
fall on the hardest rung, source-out rejections stay near zero.

We also perform a handful of smaller checks that further support these
findings
(Table [22](#A11.T22 "Table 22 ‣ Appendix K Robustness ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
Asked with no pool, Sonnet 4.6 names $`B`$ first for at most 1 of the
160 claim-disputed proposals, so recall of pre-$`T`$ papers does not
drive that set.
Appendix [F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Audit of generated ideas ‣ Appendix F Label Validation ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
reports a human audit of 60 generated ideas.

## Appendix L Natural Already-Done Ideas

A whole-idea Opus sorter, reading the eight nearest pool papers, matched
837 of the 3,000 generated ideas to a paper that already does the idea.
The claim-level labeler overruled it on 101 (these are in the
later-realized set), and 407 of the remaining 736 have the shipped
profile
(Table [27](#A12.T27 "Table 27 ‣ Appendix L Natural Already-Done Ideas ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
The set is noisier than the disguises because the sorter read exactly
the abstracts the w/o-profile ablation reads.

reports a human audit of 15 of these ideas.

## Appendix M In-the-Loop Pilot

We plug each check into a generate–check–regenerate loop on two anchors
(In-Context Edit and MoBA, 178–185-paper pools, 20 ideas each). Every
arm starts from the same first idea, and a rejection returns its reason
and cited paper to the generator, with up to three regenerations
(Table [28](#A13.T28 "Table 28 ‣ Appendix M In-the-Loop Pilot ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
A pairwise review-score proxy ([Si et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)) separates
committed from unchecked ideas on only 3 seeds for ClaimNov and 1 for
CoI-Agent, too few to compare the arms, so we leave in-the-loop
evaluation to future work.

|           |          |        |       |         |

| Arm       | 1st rej. | Checks | \$    | Seconds |
| ClaimNov  | 3/40     | 1.08   | 0.087 | 13.8    |
| CoI-Agent | 1/40     | 1.03   | 0.047 | 22.2    |
| No check  | —        | 0      | 0     | 0       |

## Appendix O Component Validations

We explain the validations we performed on each component in
§[3](#S3 "3 Novelty Module ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").

### O.1 Claim extraction

We extract typed claims from the abstract with gpt-4o-mini (temperature
0, JSON mode) using a GEPA-tuned prompt, scored against a 20-paper,
three-annotator ground truth
(Table [30](#A15.T30 "Table 30 ‣ O.1 Claim extraction ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).
When we extract from introductions rather than abstracts, F1 drops from
0.577 to 0.490, so in ClaimNov we use abstracts. gpt-5-mini has
equivalent performance on extraction but performs poorly as the
entailment judge
(Table [35](#A15.T35 "Table 35 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")).

| GEPA       | gpt-4o-mini | .674 / .695 | .793 / .744          | 38–39 |

its attribute–value text with text-embedding-3-large, then rank its
cosine similarity with same-dimension pool claims. In
Table [31](#A15.T31 "Table 31 ‣ O.2 Same-dimension retrieval ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
we score recall of the reviewer-named work on 150 ICLR 2022–23
reviewer-tell pairs with $`A`$’s own references as distractors, and in
Table [32](#A15.T32 "Table 32 ‣ O.2 Same-dimension retrieval ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
we look at the value of staying within the same dimension. Because we
find that only 3 of the 159 disputes are not in same dimension, we keep
same dimension retrieval rather than retrieving over all types of
claims.

### O.3 Graded entailment judge

In
Tables [34](#A15.T34 "Table 34 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")–[37](#A15.T37 "Table 37 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?"),
we evaluate and calibrate the graded entailment stage of ClaimNov.
Table [34](#A15.T34 "Table 34 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
compares the value of added context (specifically, titles and abstracts)
to the value of higher model tiers; we find that context is
comparatively more valuable.
Table [35](#A15.T35 "Table 35 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
investigates if the graded score alone can separate reviewer-attested
novel claims ($`n=66`$) from reviewer-attested established claims
($`n=159`$) across six judge tiers and three retrieval settings, but we
find that embedding-only similarity is a strong baseline here.
Table [36](#A15.T36 "Table 36 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
compares the judge’s use of the 1–5 entailment scale with that of three
human annotators on $`n=50`$ pairs; we find every tier agrees with the
human majority more than the annotators agree with each other.
Table [37](#A15.T37 "Table 37 ‣ O.3 Graded entailment judge ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")
tests whether our graded score can successfully rank a claim a reviewer
specifically said was novel as higher than the sibling claims from the
same paper ($`n=86`$ papers and $`n=233`$ claims); we find that it does
so above chance, 59% of the time. All in all, we observe that the graded
score can order claims well, but that there isn’t a good way to set a
pass/fail novelty threshold based off the graded score.

### O.4 Verdict

#### Calibration.

We use $`n=20`$ disputed pairs, $`n=32`$ later-realized decoys, and
$`n=106`$ already-done ideas to try and calibrate a particular novel or
non-novel threshold for $`N(P)`$, as we show in
Table [38](#A15.T38 "Table 38 ‣ Calibration. ‣ O.4 Verdict ‣ Appendix O Component Validations ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
We consider a knockout entailment level, relation labels, and a
per-candidate question; the verdict stage we ultimately adopted
considers novelty once over the whole profile
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Novelty Verdict ‣ 3 Novelty Module ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?")),
while the per-candidate question is the per-claim ablation of
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Whole-Proposal Evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ Do AI Scientists Know What’s New?").
````
